title: Apliiq for Embroidery and Patches: What to Check Before You Commit
excerpt: Embroidery and patch programs behave nothing like standard print-on-demand. Here is what to verify before you build a catalog around stitched goods, from digitizing fees to stitch count and margin.
body: Stitched decoration behaves nothing like a printed tee. A print file is cheap to change and costs the same whether it uses one color or twelve, while an embroidery file has to be digitized, every color change adds stitches, and mistakes show up as physical waste rather than a bad preview. That is why brands moving into embroidered hats, patches, and heavyweight outerwear need a different set of checks before committing a catalog to a partner. The Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing for decoration-first suppliers.

Start with digitizing. Every design has to be converted into a stitch file before a machine can read it, and that conversion is usually a one-time fee per design per size. Ask whether the fee covers revisions, whether you own the file, and whether resizing the same artwork counts as a new digitizing job. If you plan a dozen colorways of one logo, you want a partner that treats color changes as thread swaps instead of fresh setups, because that single policy can be the difference between a profitable patch program and one that never clears its setup costs.

Then look at stitch count, which is the real driver of unit cost. Dense fills and large back patches cost more than a small left-chest hit, and the price you see on a product page usually reflects a baseline stitch allowance with overage billed on top. Before you commit, price three versions of your best seller: the logo as drawn, a simplified version with fewer fills, and a small placement. Sellers are often surprised that a slightly smaller design lands twenty or thirty percent cheaper and converts just as well.

Blanks and minimums deserve the same scrutiny. Embroidery tolerates fewer garment options than printing, and heavyweight fleece, structured caps, and beanies each behave differently under a needle. Confirm which blanks are stocked, whether you can send your own, and whether custom blanks carry a minimum order. If you are building a streetwear line, the blank carries most of the perceived value, so a supplier with a thin fleece catalog quietly caps how premium your line can feel.

Lead times and quality control come next. Stitched goods take longer to produce than a printed tee, and a mistake is harder to hide, so ask how defects are handled, what photo evidence is required, and how fast a replacement ships. Order your own product before you sell it. Wear it, wash it, and check whether the backing scratches skin, because returns on embroidered items are usually about comfort rather than the artwork.

Apliiq fits brands that treat decoration as the product rather than the afterthought: private label neck tags, patches, and embroidery on premium blanks. It is a weaker choice if you need thousands of units at the lowest possible cost, or if your catalog is mostly simple one-color prints that any print partner can run. Check the current rating, pricing tiers, and decoration options on the Apliiq page at /tool/apliiq before you commit, and compare it against the other decoration-first suppliers in the Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod.
